08 · Q4 Pulse 3: pilot of the first-message codebooks

Can fresh coders apply the draft health-topic and type-of-request codebooks from the definitions alone?

Denicia Aragon Espinosa

November 05, 2026

Key points

  • What we did. We gave the draft codebooks to 3 fresh coders (separate AI sessions that never saw the drafts). Each coded the same 12 first messages using only the code definitions and rules.
  • Health topic: very consistent. All 3 coders chose the same primary topic for 12 of 12 messages (Fleiss’ κ = 1.0). Their topic matched the draft for 11 of 12.
  • Type of request: also consistent, with a few mismatches with the draft. The coders agreed on 71 of 72 yes/no code decisions (κ = 0.97). Their set of request types matched the draft for 9 of 12 messages.
  • Every evidence quote was real. 82 of 82 quotes were found word for word in the participant’s message.
  • Where the definitions were unclear. Coders were less than fully sure about 27 of 82 codes, plus 2 “no topic” decisions. Most of these were for R3 (now How do I handle this problem, or is it safe?), R6 (now Help me reach a health goal), and a message naming conditions from two topics.
  • Next step: coding every message. We proposed 9 wording edits. You approved the request edits E6, E7 and E9, and they are now applied. You first approved E8 as well, then reverted it, because emotion will be studied later in a sentiment analysis. You then renamed R3 and R6 so they are told apart by one question, problem or goal? The topic edits are no longer needed, because type of request is now the main analysis. You later added a new request type, R7 “Explain my test results”, which the pilot did not use. Both codebooks are frozen (step 09, version 5). This report describes the pilot, which was coded with the wording before those edits; the code names shown are the current ones.

1. What is a pilot, and why do one?

The draft codebooks from step 07 were built by the same process that also wrote the labels. A pilot checks whether someone new can apply the codebooks using only the written definitions. If fresh coders reach the same answers, the definitions are clear. If they hesitate or disagree, the wording needs fixing before we freeze it and code every message.

It is a small trial run on a few messages, so problems are cheap to fix.

  • Data: de-identified first messages (names replaced with [NAME]) from step 07. The homework chat excluded in step 05 is not included; the pool is the 52 included first messages.
  • Codebooks: the draft health topic codebook (T1 to T11) and type of request codebook (R1 to R6), including your review decisions from step 07.

2. Choosing the 12 pilot messages

We did not pick messages at random. A random set of 12 could easily miss the small codes. Instead, the script 08a_prepare_pilot.py (seed 8008, so it gives the same sample every time):

  1. Covered every code. It kept adding the message that covered the most codes not yet in the sample, until every topic, every request type, and the “no topic” and “no request type” options appeared at least once.
  2. Added hard cases. It filled the rest with messages that were tricky in step 07: the 3 drafting passes disagreed, or you recoded them in your review.
sample |>
  transmute(pilot_order, chat_id, n_words, why_chosen,
            first_message = mask_names(str_trunc(text, 160))) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(pilot_order = "#", chat_id = "Chat", n_words = "Words", why_chosen = "Why chosen",
             first_message = "First message (first 160 characters)") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(16), data_row.padding = px(8))

3. A codebook-only prompt

Each coder received the same instructions (prompts\pilot_coding_prompt.md) and the same codebook (codebook\pilot_codebook.md). The codebook contains only:

  • the code names and definitions;
  • the signs to look for, and how each code differs from its nearest neighbour (close-call rules);
  • example quotes;
  • the “none” options;
  • the rules: one primary health topic plus an optional secondary topic, and one or more request types per message.

The coders never saw the draft labels. We also hid any example quote that came from one of the 12 pilot messages (12 examples). Otherwise a coder could match the quote rather than apply the definition.

For every code they gave, each coder had to supply:

  • an evidence quote copied word for word from the message;
  • a confidence rating: high, medium or low;
  • an “unclear because…” note whenever the definitions did not clearly decide the case.

4. Three independent coders

Three separate AI coder sessions coded the 12 messages. None could see the others’ work. Each got the messages in its own shuffled order (seeds 8101, 8102, 8103), so the order of messages could not push all 3 towards the same answer. Every prompt, input file and raw answer is saved in output\08_pilot-codebook\coders\ and input\.

5. Quote check

A script checked every evidence quote against the participant’s message. This catches a coder “remembering” words that are not there.

if (n_quotes_ok == n_quotes) {
  cat(sprintf("All %d evidence quotes were found word for word in the message.", n_quotes))
} else {
  quotes |> filter(!quote_found) |> gt() |> tab_options(table.font.size = px(16))
}
## All 82 evidence quotes were found word for word in the message.

6. Did the 3 coders agree with each other?

Fleiss’ kappa (κ) measures agreement among several coders, after allowing for agreement expected by chance. A κ of 1 means perfect agreement; 0 means no better than chance. Above about 0.8 is usually read as very strong.

  • Health topic: one primary topic per message, so κ compares the 3 coders’ primary topics.
  • Type of request: a message can have several types. So for every message and every request type, each coder made a yes/no decision, and κ is pooled over those decisions.
agreement |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(measure = "Measure", value = "Result") |>
  tab_options(table.font.size = px(17), data_row.padding = px(8))
Measure Result
Topic: primary topic, Fleiss' kappa among 3 pilot coders 1.0
Topic: messages where all 3 coders chose the same primary topic 12 of 12
Topic: messages where 2+ coders chose the same primary topic 12 of 12
Topic: pilot majority primary topic = draft primary topic 11 of 12
Request: pooled Fleiss' kappa (every message x code yes/no decision) 0.97
Request: message x code decisions where all 3 coders agreed 71 of 72
Request: messages where all 3 coders gave exactly the same set of types 11 of 12
Request: pilot majority set of types = draft set 9 of 12
Quote check: evidence quotes found word for word 82 of 82
Codes given with medium or low confidence 29 of 82
'Unclear because...' notes written 29

A note of caution. With only 12 messages, κ can jump a lot with a single change, so treat these numbers as a rough check. Also, the pilot coders and the step-07 drafting passes are the same AI model, so they may share blind spots. Agreement among them may therefore be higher than between two people. Your own hand-coding (section 10) would be the stronger test.

What the differences mean:

  • 69f4ca1a names PCOS, anemia, PMDD and high cholesterol, and asks for a supplement. All 3 coders made Pregnancy and reproductive health (T10) the primary topic, with Diabetes and hormones (T6) secondary. The draft had them the other way round. The current rule assumes the message centres on one condition, so it could not settle this case. For the request, 2 of 3 coders added R3 (then Ask what to do for relief, now How do I handle this problem, or is it safe?) to R6 (then Personal plan or recommendations, now Help me reach a health goal), because the supplement is meant to treat named conditions.
  • 6a0206ae (“what’s stressing me out and why I’m anxious”). All 3 coders added Ask what is causing symptoms (R1) to the draft’s R3. They all noted that R1 is written around physical symptoms.
  • 69d51123 (“Should you be drinking 3 weeks after … surgery”). The draft gave no request type. All 3 coders gave R3, following the rule that “should I do X” questions go to R3, but they said R3’s wording (about relief) fits only weakly.

8. Where did the definitions cause hesitation?

The chart counts, for each code, how often a coder gave it with medium or low confidence. These are the places where a definition did not settle the case on its own.

conf_plot <- codes |>
  filter(code != "NONE", confidence %in% c("medium", "low")) |>
  count(code, confidence) |>
  left_join(names07, by = "code") |>
  mutate(label = paste0(code, "  ", name),
         confidence = factor(str_to_sentence(confidence), levels = c("Low", "Medium"))) |>
  group_by(label) |> mutate(total = sum(n)) |> ungroup() |>
  mutate(label = reorder(label, total))

p_conf <- ggplot(conf_plot, aes(n, label, fill = confidence)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Medium = project_colors[["clay"]], Low = project_colors[["teal"]]),
                    breaks = c("Medium", "Low"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = scales::breaks_pretty(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "Codes given with medium or low confidence (3 coders × 12 messages)", y = NULL,
       title = "Where coders were less than sure") +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
p_conf

save_fig("pilot-confidence-by-code", p_conf, width = 11, height = 7)

Codes not shown were always given with high confidence. Below are all the “unclear because…” notes, grouped by message. Many notes repeat across the 3 coders, which is a strong sign that the wording, not the coder, is the problem.

Gaps the coders pointed out (from their overall feedback):

  • No topic covers the kidneys, bladder, liver or blood. All 3 coders flagged the kidney ultrasound report (6a638cf5) and anemia.
  • Only one secondary topic is allowed, which clashes with the diet/supplement rule when a message also names conditions from two topics.
  • Emotional questions (“why am I anxious”) do not clearly fit request types written around physical symptoms.

9. Proposed wording edits and your decisions

These are proposals only. The step-07 codebooks have not been changed. The full table, with the current and proposed wording side by side, is in 08_proposed_edits.csv and in the proposed_edits sheet of 08_Q4_3_pilot_results.xlsx.

Update after your decision on the analysis. You chose to make type of request the main analysis and to treat health topics as a simple descriptive list (one primary topic per message; see the step 07 report). That makes the topic edits E1, E3, E4 and E5 unnecessary. E2 is handled simply: the kidney report gets a Kidney, liver and blood line in the topic list. With only 1 message, that line is shown under Other health subject. You then approved the request edits E6, E7 and E9, and they are applied to the request codebook (step 07, revisions 9 to 12). E8 was reverted (revisions 13 and 14): emotion is not part of any request type, because it will go into the sentiment analysis later. The Mental health and stress topic stays. Finally, you renamed and clarified R3 and R6 (revisions 15 and 16), because “what should I do” and “recommendations” sounded too alike, and “personal” fits all health advice. They are now told apart by one question, problem or goal? R3, “How do I handle this problem, or is it safe?”, starts from a symptom, injury or condition the person already has and wants to treat, manage or stay safe with. R6, “Help me reach a health goal”, starts from a goal such as weight, fitness or a routine, with nothing to fix, and wants a plan. The meaning of E6, E7 and E9 is unchanged. The Status column shows what happened to each edit; the shaded rows are the applied ones.

10. Optional: code the pilot messages yourself

08_hand-coding_sheet.xlsx lists the 12 pilot messages with drop-down menus for the primary topic, the secondary topic and up to 3 request types. A definitions sheet holds the full codebook. Its request list now also offers R7 “Explain my test results” (added after the pilot; your entries were kept). It shows no labels from the AI coders or the draft, so you code blind.

This is optional. If you do it, we can compare your codes with the AI coders’. A person agreeing with the codebook is the best evidence that the definitions work.

You have started it (10 of 12 messages coded). When R3 and R6 were renamed, your sheet was updated in place. Your answers, the drop-down lists and the definitions sheet now use the new names, and your choices themselves are unchanged. A copy of your sheet from before the rename is in old\. The script never overwrites this sheet once it exists.

  1. Your review: done. You approved request edits E6, E7 and E9, reverted E8, and renamed R3 and R6 around problem vs. goal. The topic edits are no longer needed, because topics are now a descriptive list. Hand-coding the 12 messages is still optional.
  2. Apply and freeze: done. The changes are applied in step 07 (revisions 9 to 16; later revisions 17 to 24 added the first real message rule and R7 “Explain my test results”). The final codebooks are locked in output/09_freeze-codebook/frozen_2026-11-05_v5/ (step 09). Version 1 (still had E8), version 2 (old R3 and R6 names), version 3 (before the first real message rule) and version 4 (before R7) are marked superseded. After this, the wording no longer changes.
  3. Next: code every included first message (52) three times with the frozen codebooks, then measure agreement and take the majority label. This waits for your go-ahead.

Files

Scripts (scripts\08_pilot-codebook\)

  • 08a_prepare_pilot.py: chooses the sample, writes the codebook-only text, and writes each coder’s shuffled input and prompt.
  • prompts\pilot_coding_prompt.md: the coder instructions template.
  • 08b_check_pilot.py: quote check, agreement, pilot vs draft, the results workbook and the hand-coding sheet.
  • 08_Q4_3_pilot-codebook.Rmd: this report.

Results (output\08_pilot-codebook\)

  • input\: pilot_sample.csv (draft labels kept for comparison only; never shown to coders), pilot_settings.json (seeds), coder_orders.csv, and coder_1/2/3_input.txt.
  • codebook\pilot_codebook.md: the exact codebook text the coders saw.
  • coders\: each coder’s full prompt and raw JSON answer.
  • pilot_agreement.csv, pilot_by_code.csv, pilot_vs_draft.csv, pilot_codes_long.csv, pilot_unclear_notes.csv, pilot_quote_check.csv and pilot_coder_feedback.csv.
  • 08_proposed_edits.csv: the proposed edits, with a status column (E6, E7 and E9 applied; E8 reverted). old\ holds earlier versions.
  • 08_Q4_3_pilot_results.xlsx: all of the above in one workbook.
  • 08_hand-coding_sheet.xlsx: the optional blind hand-coding sheet, which you have partly filled in (never overwritten by the script).
  • figures\: the confidence chart.
